title: Strict hot spots and absence of interior critical points on smooth simply connected planar domains
main_claim: Every nonzero first-positive Neumann eigenfunction on a smooth bounded simply connected planar domain has a gradient that never vanishes in the interior, even when the eigenvalue is multiple. Hence the strict hot spots conclusion holds. The proof runs as follows. Rohleder's vector principle (Q(X) >= mu||X||^2 on tangent fields, with equality exactly for gradients in V) is pulled back conformally to give a PSD boundary energy E with E(g)=0. A multiplier identity follows: E(bg) = 1/2 ∬ N (b(s)-b(t))^2 g(s)·g(t). The core kernel theorem says D_p = K(p,s)K(p,t)/N(s,t) is conditionally negative semidefinite, proved via reciprocal matrices with at most one positive eigenvalue (McCullough–Quiggin type). Schoenberg's embedding then gives Σ_j E(b_j g) = 1/2|∇u(Φ(p))|^2. A critical point would therefore produce too many eigenfunction gradients, contradicting either dim V <= 2 or unique continuation.
coverage:
I read every section in full and checked each step.
Section 2: the Filonov gap mu<lambda_D; the conformal map; the boundary weight beta (Green identity signs checked); connected sign sets; the dim<=2 argument via the cosine function F.
Section 3: the Helmholtz decomposition; Z=∇r using simple connectivity; the Poincaré inequalities and the equality case; the curvature identity (2 det ∇X and a^2 κ checked by hand).
Section 4: the kernel bounds; the energy normalization ∫|∇z^m|^2 = 2π|m| = 1/2·(1/π)·(2π)^2|m|; the sign of the R term; the multiplier identity, expanded by hand (the N0 and R terms both give +1/2(b_s-b_t)^2 g_s·g_t).
Section 5: the log-mean integral and the c_α normalization (sin πα/π); the identity h(h+1)/(h+r) = h + (1-r) - r(1-r)/(h+r); the Lorentz form of h+1/2; the geometric series k/(1-(1-r)k) = 1/(h+r); the rank-one update lemma, including the series for a/(1+ca) - H/(1+cH); the chain/Schur elimination formula; the quadrature, ε, radial and ρ limits (asymptotics G/(1-r)→P_s and G/(1-r)^2→N0 checked); the bordered-matrix ⇒ CND step.
Section 6: Schoenberg's construction, dominated convergence, and both endgame cases.
Numerics: I tested Theorem 5.1 independently on the disk with constant potentials q = c dx (c = 0.05 to 5.5, near the critical value j_{0,1}^2). I computed R from its exact Fourier coefficients k J_{m+1}(k)/(2π J_m(k)), with the 1/m log singularity summed in closed form, and K from J_m(kr)/J_m(k) by recurrence. For p = 0 to 0.99, all eigenvalues of the 400-point matrices restricted to the sum-zero subspace were <= 0, up to about 1e-7 rounding. Naive truncation produced spurious positive eigenvalues, which went away once the series were computed accurately.
sibling_notes: There were no prior entries in the family 369 hash. The kernel theorem (Thm 5.1) is stated for any bounded nonnegative subcritical disk potential, so companion papers could reuse it. If anyone checks it numerically, note that R(s,t) has a logarithmic diagonal singularity (Fourier coefficients ~ c/(4πm)): truncated sums give false positive eigenvalues.
